text: Numeration, Addition, Subtraction, Mul[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tiplication Diuiſion, Progreſſion, and extra[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ction of rootes: to theſe ſome men adde Du[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]plation, Triplation, and Mediation. But as for theſe laſte thrée, they are contained vnder the other ſeauen. For Duplation and Tri[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]plation, are contained vnder Multiplication, as it ſhall appeare in their place. And Media[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tion is contained vnder Diuiſion, as I wyl declare in his place alſo.

So you knowe nowe both howe to adde two ſu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]mes or more together: and al[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſo how to proue whether you haue done well or no:Addition of nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]bers of diuerſe denomi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]nations. which thing alſo you may doe beſt by Subtraction. But becauſe you cannot yet ſkil of it, I will let that paſſe till anone, and will teache you now how to adde ſu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]mes of diuers denominations: whiche thing can neuer be but whe[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] the one denomination is ſuch that it conteineth the other certain times. And yet you ſhal adde them to the other, not after this ſort as you did them that were of one deno[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]mination, but after ſuch a ſort as I will now ſhew you, that is to ſay.

THen haue I learned the two firſt kindes of Arithmetike: nowe as I remember, doeth fo[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]lowe Subtraction, whoſe name me thin[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]keth doth ſounde con[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]trarie to Addition.

So is it in déede: for as Addition encreaſeth one groſſe ſumme by bringing manye into one, ſo contrarie waies, Sub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]traction diminiſheth a groſſe ſumme by with[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]drawing of other from it, ſo that Subtracti[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]on or Rebating is nothing elſe, but an art to withdrawe and abate one ſumme from an o[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ther, that the Remainer may appeare.

And as for this worde that you laſte aſked me, take you this deſcription:Remainer. The Remai[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ner is a ſumme lefte after due Subtraction made, which declareth the exceſſe or differe[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]ce of the two other numbers: as if I woulde abate or ſubtract 14 out of 18, there ſhould re[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]maine 4, which is called the remayner, and is the difference betwéen thoſe two numbers 14 & 18.
I perceiue then what Subtracti[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]on is: Nowe reſteth to knowe the order to worke it,
Nowe will I proue in a greater ſumme: And I wil Subtract 2367924 out of 3468946. Thoſe ſummes I ſet in order thus. [GAP:math]
Thys is well done. And that you maye be ſure to perceiue fullye the Art of Subtractio[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]. let me ſee how can you ſubtract 52984732 out of 8250003456.

Then ſhall I ſaye becauſe I borrowed 10 to the ouer 5, I muſte put in the next place beneath, that is vnder 2: then muſt I ſubtracte that [GAP:illegible] from [GAP:illegible], and there re[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſteth 1, to be written vnder that, in the ninth place. Nowe I haue no more to ſubtracte, for there is neuer any figure remayning be[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]neath, nether yet any vnite to be added, be[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]cauſe I borrowed not 10 to the figure laſte before,☞ and yet is there 8 remayning in the ouer line, which (I thinke by reaſon) ſhoulde be ſet at the ende of the figures in the loweſt row whiche is vnder the line, for becauſe there was nothing taken from it.

Yea, what elſe? Whether they bée one or many: and this wel remembred, you haue ſufficiently learned Subtractio[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]. How be it, becauſe of certaine thinges that might deceiue you, if you did not take good héede to your working, I wil propoſe to you another example of many numbers to be ſubtracted, as thus,

Then firſte I begin at the firſt place, & ga[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ther togither the ſum of al thoſe lynes (ſaue the ouermoſt) in their firſt figures, and ſo do I with all the figures of the ſecond place, & ſo forth as I did in Ad[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]dition, ſaue that I leaue out the higheſt row of numbers (as the line warneth me) and that ſumme ſo gathered betwéen the double line, doe I ſubtract out of the higheſt row of numbers, and the remayner doe I ſette vn[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]der ye nethermoſt line: [GAP:math] as for example.

Then come I to ſubtracting of this ſu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]me betwéene the lines, for by Addition it is e[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]quall to the fiue parcels ouer it. Therefore I procéede to ſubtracte it from the ouermoſte ſumme, ſaying: 2 from 9, remayne 7, to bée written vnder the[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] beneath the loweſt line. Then in the ſeconde place I take 5 from 6, and there reſteth, to be written vnder the[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]. Then in the third place, 4 from 8, reſteth 4. Laſt of all in the fourth place, 1 from 2, re[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]mayneth 1. And thus I ſée that after thoſe 5 ſummes are ſubtracted from 2869, the Re[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]mainer is 1417.

Yes,An a[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]bridgeme[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]t of the for[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]mer maner of Subtra[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ction. when you are a while ex[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]erciſed in it: for you may as faſt as you can gather the numbers togither, withdrawe them out of the higheſt ſu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]me if ſo be it, that all the parcels which you doe gather, do not excéede nine, but and if they excéede nyne, then muſt you ſubtract onelye the digit that is in it, and reſerue the article till the nexte place, where you ſhall adde it with the other figures and ſo ſubtract the whole out of the figure aboue them: but and if in this place the ſumme of the parcels do excéede 9, then (as I ſayd before) ſubtract the digit only, and reſerue the article to the nexte place, and ſo ſtill goe forth, till you haue ended your working.

Than doe thus: [GAP:illegible] ſtill as you gather your parcels, when they excéed a digit, & ma[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]keth him 10 or more, take the article, and write him betwéene two lines (as in the firſt example) vnder the next place towarde the left hande: and then deducte the digitte from the figure that is ouer him, and wryte the remayner. And then when you gather the next parcels, you ſhall adde to them the figure that is vnder them, betwéen the two lines. And if it excéede 9, do as I ſaid before, write the article vnder ye next place betwéen ye lynes, and ſubtracte the digitte from the Figure that is ouer thoſe parcelles: and if that all the parcelles togither and the num[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ber betwéene the lines do make but a digit, then deduct it wholy from the figure aboue: as in this example. I would ſubtracte oute of 40308964, [GAP:math] theſe thrée parcelles

I commende you for your re[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]membraunce. And truth it is, I ſhould not haue ſet them here, but only becauſe that I would make you plainly to perceiue the art of Subtraction. Therfore ſéeing that you do now perceiue it, whenſoeuer you ſhoulde write downe a cyphar, looke whether anye other figures be yet behinde. And if not than let go the cyphar alſo, for it néedeth notto write him in any latter places, where no other figure doth followe, excepte it be (as I did) to teache the vſe of Subtraction the playner.
So I woulde thinke by yt you taughte me before. And now I beléeue I could ſubtract any ſummes.

So may you if you haue mar[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ked what I haue taught you. But becauſe this thing (as all other) muſt be learned ſurely by often practiſe, I will propounde here two examples to you, wherein if you often exerciſe your ſelfe, you ſhalbe ripe and perfecte to ſubtract any other ſumme lightly, for in them is contained all the obſeruaun[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ces of whole number. And becauſe you ſhal perceaue ſomewhat both how to doe it, and alſo whether it be well done when you haue prooued to doe it, therefore haue I written vnder them, both the Remayners: And to one of them alſo adioyned his proofe.
Then I truſt by practiſe to at[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]taine the vſe of it. And is this all that I ſhall learne of Subtraction?

This doe I perceiue verie well, and if there be none other thing to be learned in Subtraction, then maye I come to Multi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]plication, for that you reckened to bée in or[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]der next.

We haue done in déede wyth the arte of Subtraction, as touching the wor[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]king. But yet before we go to multiplication,A proofe of Subtra[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ction in numbers of one deno[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]mination. I wil inſtruct you how to examine your work whether it be well done or no, and that is by caſting away 9 as ofte[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] as you can finde it, as you did in Addition, ſauing that you muſte here examine the higheſt number alone, and note the reſidue of it at a lines end, as you did in Addition.

And if you will you may make for euerye denomination a line, as you learned in Ad[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]dition: but then muſt you beginne your ex[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]amination at the ſmalleſt denomination, as you did in Addition, for their proofe is alto[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]gither like, ſauing that in Addition you ex[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]amine the nethermoſt ſumme alone, and all the other togither: and in Subtraction yée muſt examine the higheſt number alone, & al the other togither. And if you marke it wel, it is euen all one, for that ſumme that in Ad[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]dition is loweſt, in Subtraction is higheſt:Groſſe or total ſume[CHAR:char:punc] and that ſumme is called the Groſſe or To[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tall ſumme.

Therefore if you marke what I ſayde in Addition, you may eaſilye perceiue what is to be done for the proofe of Subtractio[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]. And to the intent that you may perceaue it ye bet[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ter, I will ſhew you an other proofe of Sub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]traction, and that ſhall be by Addition, thus. Draw vnder ye loweſt nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]ber (which is your remayner) a line: then ad that number,An other proofe of Subtractio[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]. and all the other that you did ſubtract before, to[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]gether, and write that that amounteth, vnder the loweſt line: and if the ſumme that com[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]meth thereof, be equall to the higheſt of the ſubtraction, than was the [GAP:math] ſubtraction well wrought, or elſe not. As for exam[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ple: in the laſte ſummes, which ſtoode thus.
And thus nowe haue I [GAP:math] taughte you the arte of Subtraction, and the means to proue whether it be well wroughte or not.

And this laſt proofe of Subtraction is moſt ap[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]teſt and beſte allowed of any other proofe: whe[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ther it be of lb ſ d. or a[CHAR:char:EOLunhyphen]ny other groſſe ſome whatſoeuer.
Nowe and you remember, I omitted in teaching the proofe of Addition one way whi: che I ſaid was by ſubtraction.

Trueth it is, and then was it de[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ferred, becauſe that I had not the[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] learned the feate of Subtraction, whereby I ſhould haue proued it, but now I thanke you, I haue wel learned the arte of Subtraction, & the proues of it, both by 9. and by addition. And nowe I would be glad to know, howe I may proue Addition by Subtraction.

Then marke you this.The profe of Additi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]on by Sub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]traction. Whe[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] you haue ended your addition: take the numbers all that you did adde, to the higheſt ſumme, and deduct or ſubtract them from the groſſe ſumme that doth reſulte, and if the remay[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ner be like to the higheſt number, then haue you done well, elſe not.

Then doe I come to the middle number (becauſe here in this example are onelye thrée numbers) and ſubtracte that from the nether nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]ber, beginning at the right hande, and firſt I ſaye, 0 out of 0, there remaineth 0: that write I vnder an other line. Then againe, 0 in the ſecond place from 0, remai[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]neth 0 vnder it I write 0 alſo. Next that in the third place, 4 out of 2 wil not be, therfore I ad to that 2, 10, and make it 12 from that I take 4 and there reſteth 8. Then ſaye I farther: 9 in the fourth place, and 1 (whiche I muſt adde for the 10, borrowed before) make 10, that muſt I take from 6: and be[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]cauſe I canne not, I adde to the 6.10, and then is it 16: from then I take 10, and there reſteth 6. to be written vnder them. Againe in the fift place where I finde nothing writ[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ten, I muſt ſette 1 for the 10 laſt borrowed, and that 1 doe I take from the 1 vnder him, and ſo remaineth noughte, wherefore I write downe a cypher 0. Now haue I done with the ſubtraction: and yet in the groſſe ſumme remayneth 1, whiche I muſt ſette right in the ſame place, in the remayner, and ſo the remayner appeareth to bee lyke vnto the higheſt ſumme of [GAP:math] the Addition, as here ap[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]peareth. Wherefore I ſay that the Additio[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] was wel wroughte. And note, that if you had ſubtracted the vppermoſt from the product or totall ſu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]me, then the reſidue thereof woulde be equall to that middlemoſt number. But if the parcelles which you added, be more then two: (as thrée foure, fiue, ſixe, or more) than from your groſſe or totall ſumme ſubtracte firſt one of the percels: and note that newe reſidue. Out of that new reſidue, ſubtract an other of your percels, (whiche you will) and Note that ſecond new reſidue. And if you haue no mo percels added, but three, than is that ſecond new reſidue equall & alike to the thirde parcel, whiche you haue not (as yet) ſubtracted, if you haue wrought wel: both in your firſt Addition, and now in youre ſub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tracting. And ſo in this wiſe, (if you haue foure, fiue, or more parcels) maye you pro[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]céede to make your ſelfe ſure of your totall ſumme, firſt, by Addition of the ſaide par[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]cels, produced and gathered. And thus may you doe in any other ſumme of one denomi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]nation or many: Sauing that I wil tel you by the way, the laſte manner of proofe that was ſhewed you in Addition, is the beſte, and the apteſt proofe for the Rule of Addi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tion.
Therefore nowe will I make an ende of Subtraction, and will inſtructe you in Multiplication.☞
That is commonly vſed by ye proofe of 9, as you learned before in Addition and Subtraction, ſaue that it hath this wayes diuers from them.

Diuiſion vvhat it is.Diuiſion is a diſtributing of a greater ſumme by the vnities of a leſſer Or Diuiſion is an Arithmetical producing of a thyrde number, in reſpect of two propounded numbers: which thirde number ſhal ſo ofte[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] containe an vnit, as the greater of the two propounded numbers doth contain the leſſer. So that, euen as Multiplication did ſéeme to ſerue in ſtéede of manye Additions, ſo Diui[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſion maye ſeeme to be in place of many Sub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tractions: Bicauſe that third number briefly expreſſeth, how many times the leſſer of your two propounded nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]bers may be Subtracted, from ye greater: As in practiſe wil more plain[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ly appeare. Therefore (as you may perceyue) vnto Diuiſion are required three nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]bers: the firſt, which ſhould be diuided, and that muſte (generally) be the greater: and the ſeconde, by which the other muſt be diuided, and that is (generallie) the leſſer, & is called ye Diuiſor. And the thirde which aunſwereth to the que[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſtion, How many times: and therefore is cal[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]led the Quotient.

Then do I take 8 as many times out of 2[GAP:illegible], ſaying: 3 times 8 make 24, and if I take 24 out of 25, there remaineth 1: [GAP:math] ſo then I cancell 25 and 8, and ouer the 5 I ſet 1, thus. Or you mought (after you founde 3 to be a fit quotie[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]t) ſtraight way haue multi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]plied the whole diuiſor 28, by that 3, at once: which giueth 84, whiche being ſet vnder 28, and duelie ſubtracted from 85, [GAP:math] of the number diuided, gi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ueth 1, ye remainer of ye whole diuiſion: as before you hadde. Worke which waye you liſt: here you ſée alſo the forme.

And marke, when ſoeuer it chanceth ſo, yt you ſhould ſet forwarde the diuiſor, and that it can not ſtande there, bycauſe there is no nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] [CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ber ouer the laſte place, or if there be any, it is leſſer then the laſte figure of the diuiſor,☜ then muſt you remoue the diuiſor yet once again: and becauſe that his firſte place of remouing ſerued not to ſubtracte him ſo much as once, therefore ſhal you write in the quotient a Ci[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]pher 0. And if you ſhould by chaunce néede to do ſo ofte[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]times, for euerie time write a cipher in the quoitente. The reaſon of this, will I ſhew you hereafter.
Borow of the next number that is be[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]hinde (for there is 230) and doe as you lear[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ned in Subtraction in a like caſe.

Note.You néede not goe about to mul[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tiplie when the Quotient is 1, for 1 doth nei[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ther multiplie nor diuide, but in ſuch caſe on[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ly ſubtract the diuiſor out of the number that is ouer it,

So is it: and as often as you ſeeke in the table and finde your number iuſt,Marke the diuerſitie be[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tvveene a true quotient and a iuſt quotient. the di[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]git againſt it is your true and iuſt quotiente. I cal that a true quotient alſo, if it be ye right quotient that you ſhoulde take[GAP:illegible] though your diuiſor multiplied by the ſame, do not cleare[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ly ſubtract the number ouer it, but there doth ſomewhat remaine, as it chaunced in al the examples that you did worke by. But if it ſhoulde ch[GAP:illegible]nce (as it doth often) that your di[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]uiſor multiplied by your quotient, do ſubtract clean the number ouer it, the[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] cal I that quo[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tient not only a true quotient, but alſo a iuſte quotient, becauſe it doth iuſtlie conſume the number ouer the diuiſor: and that chaunceth euermore when the nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]ber ouer the diuiſor is iuſtly found in the table.

When you haue founde in the table, other the ſame ſum that is ouer the diuiſor, other ye next beneath, (for lack of the other) the[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] loke what digit ſtandeth againſte it, take that for your quotient. And bicauſe it is ſome paine to multiply the diuiſor by the quotient, you ſhal not neede to doe it, but only take the number that you founde in the table, and ſubtract that from the ouer number: for if you do multiply the diuiſor by the quotient, that will be the number that ſhal amounte, therefore is this way more eaſier.

Then ſet I forwarde the [GAP:math] diuiſor, and finde ouer it 144, as appeareth [GAP:illegible]: then ſéeke I ye number in the ta[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ble and finde it, and againſt it is 6, therefore I ſet 6 before 1 for my quo[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tient, and I take that 144 for the iuſte mul[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tiplication of the diuiſor by that quotient, and therefore without any newe [GAP:math] multiplication I do ſubtract the 144, from the other 144, and there reſteth nothing, as you may ſée.

The ſecond rule is this. From the laſt ſubtract the firſt, the remainer diuide by the common exceſſe, to the Quotient ad 1, and you haue the number of the places, which you wold know: As in this progreſ[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſion.

If I know only 6 and 31, and that they en[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]creaſe by 5, than according to the rule, from 31 I ſubtract 6, there remaineth 25, which 25 I diuide by 5 (the common exceſſe) the quotient commeth forth 5, to which I ad 1, that maketh 6: and ſo many are the places, as you ſée.

The third propoſition may alwaies thus be ſoluted: Multiplye the exceſſe by a number leſſe by 1. than the diſtaunce of the place is from the firſt or the laſt number gi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]uen: the of come ad to the firſt, if the diſtance be reckned from the firſt, and the firſte alſo known or ſubtract from the laſt: if the di[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſtaunce be from the laſt counted, and ye laſte giuen alſo, and that whiche commeth forth, either in that addition to the firſt, or ſubtra[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ction from the laſt, is the number ſought As for example I propound you this progreſ[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſion.

Now, if that exceſſe whereby this Pro[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]greſſion ſtandeth, be knowne to be 7, and the firſt number giuen, being 8, I woulde know what number ſtandeth vnder 4, that is to ſay in the fourth place. I multiplie 7 by 3 (which is leſſe by 1, than the number of the place propounded) that yéeldeth 21, to which I adde 8 (the firſt number) ſo com[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]meth 29: which I ſay to belo[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]g to the fourth place, as ye ſée in the example it alſo doeth: or if in the third place from the laſt, you would know what number in this example ſhould ſtand, the laſt number being known to be 57, and the common exceſſe 7, than by 2 (which is leſſe by 1 than the place propou[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] [CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ded) I multiplie 7, that giueth 14: whiche I ſubtract from 57, ſo remaineth 43: which appertaineth to the thirde place incluſiuely reckned from the laſt, & ſo my example gi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ueth you.

The fift propoſition hath this rule appertaining vnto it: By the fourthe rule finde the number of the places, that béeing done, from the laſt ſubtract the firſte, and the reſidue diuide by a number leſſe by 1, than the number of the places, and the quotient will ſhewe the exceſſe whiche is ſought for.

Nowe I thinke beſte that you paſſe forthe to Subtraction, excepte there be anye wayes to examine this manner of Addition, then I thinke that were good to be knowen next.

No, not with one finger, howe be it, with diuerſe fingers you maye expreſſe 9999. and al at one time, & that lacketh but 1 of 10000. And as for Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, and Diuiſion (whiche yet were neuer taught by any man as farre as I doe knowe) I will inſtruct you after the trea[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tiſe of Fractions: and now for this time fare well, and looke that you ceaſſe not to practiſe that you haue learned.

If there be no more difficultie in their Nu[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]meration, the[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] I pray you go forward to their Addition and Subtraction,☜ and ſo to the other kinds of workes for I vnderſtande that the ſame kinds of workes be in Fractions, that be in whole numbers.

Therefore ſome men (as Stifelius) doe expreſſe without a line numbers of proporti[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]on, being applied to Addition or Subtracti[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]on: becauſe they muſt be take[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] as two, where the line in Fractions maketh them to be ta[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ken for one: for of the Numeratour and De[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]nominatour is made one number.

This is plainely expreſſed, and truely and hereby (I doubte not) but you doe perceiue, yt as great a differe[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]ce as is betwéen 16 & 76, ſo much differe[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]ce is betwéene theſe two Fractions 4/9 and ⅖: and 4/9 of ⅖. And now that you vnderſtande theſe varie[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ties, I will procéede to the reſt of the works: firſt admoniſhing you, that there is an other order to be followed in Fractions than there was in whole numbers, for in whole num[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]bers this was the order: Numeration, Addi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tion, Subtraction, Multiplication, Diuiſion, and Reduction, but in Fractions (to followe the ſame aptneſſe in procéeding from the eaſi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]eſt workes to the harder) we muſt vſe this order of the workes: Numeration, Multipli[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]cation, Diuiſion, Reduction, Addition, and Subtraction.

That Multiplication and Diuiſion ſhoulde goe togither, and Subtraction to followe Addition, naturall order doeth per[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſwade: but why Multiplication ſhoulde be firſt in order here next to Numeration, and Reduction in the middle, I deſire to vnder[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſtand the reaſon

As in the Arte of whole numbers order woulde reaſonablye beginne with the eaſieſt, and ſo goe forwarde by degrées to the hardeſt, euen ſo reaſon teacheth in Fractions the like order. And conſidering that Addition or Subtraction of Fractions can very ſeldom be wrought without multiplication and Re[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]duction: and contrariwayes, Multiplication and Reductio[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] may be wrought without this forme of Addition or Subtraction. But & if the fractio[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]s be not of one denomina[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tion, or any of them be mixt of whole nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]bers and fractions, then muſt you firſt reduce them to one denomination, and after adde them. And if they be manye, then adde firſt two of them, and to the ſum that doth amount of the Addition, add the third, and then the fourth, & ſo forth, if you haue ſo many.
Now may we go to ſubtraction.

SVbtraction hathe the ſame precepts that ad[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]dition hadde, for if the Denominatours bée like, then muſte you ſubtracte the one nu[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]meratour from the o[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ther, and the reſt is to be ſet ouer the common denominator, and ſo your Subtraction is ended: but and if you haue manye Fractions to be ſubtracted out of many, then muſt you reduce them to one de[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]nomination, and into two ſeueral Fractions, that is, all that muſte be ſubtracted into one Fraction, and the reſidue into an other Fraction, and then worke as I ſayde bée[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]fore.

Then do I adde the two firſt, & they make 3[GAP:illegible]/19[GAP:illegible]. Alſo I adde the two laſte, and they yéeld [GAP:illegible]08/162[GAP:illegible] Then doe I ſubtract 3040 out of 3408, and there reſteth 368, ſo is the remainer [GAP:illegible]68/1920 that is in ſmaller Tearmes, 23/120. I take theſe two Fractions, ⅞ and 7/24, which being reduced, wil ſta[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]d thus, 168/192. & 72/191 Now would I ſubtract 168 out of 72, but I can not.

Then maye you perceiue that you miſtooke the Fractions: for you ca[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] neuer ſub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tract the greater out of the leſſer, althoughe you may adde, multiplie or diuide the greater with the leſſer. But and you ſhould ſubtract a fraction out of a whole number what would you do?
Marrie I woulde reduce the whole nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] [CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ber into a Fraction of the ſame Denomina[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tion that my Fraction is, and then worke by Subtraction.

So may you doe, but it is eaſier much, if your fraction be a proper fraction, that is to ſay, leſſe then an Vnite, to take an Vnite fro[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] the whole number, and then turne it into an Improper Fraction[CHAR:char:punc] and ſo worke your ſub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]traction. As if I woulde ſubtracte ⅗ from 4, I maye take one from 4, and turne it into 5/5, from whiche if I bate 7/6, there will remayne 3 ⅖: And if the firſte fraction be an Improper Fraction, then may I take ſo manye Vnites from the whole number, that they may make an improper fraction greater then that firſte, and then worke by Subtraction: As if there be proponed 10/3 to be ſubtracted fro[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] 6, becauſe [GAP:illegible]0/3 is more than 3, and not ſo much as 4. Or, elſe you may at your pleaſure take 3 ⅓ whiche is 10/3 from 6 whole: Then ſet one vnder 6. as thus 6/1: And then to reduce thoſe 2 fractions into one Denomination as [GAP:math] here appeareth:

Then beginne againe, and take an other number whiche ſhall be called the Seconde poſition, and worke by the queſtion: if you haue miſſed again, note the exceſſe or default as it is, and call that the ſecond errour. Then multiply croſſe waies the firſt poſition by the ſecond errour, and againe the ſeconde poſiti[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]on by the firſte errour, and note their totalls ſeuerally by the names of Totalles. Then marke whether the two errours were bothe like, that is to ſay, both too much, or bothe too little: or whether they be vnlike, that is, the one too much, and the other too little, for if they be like, then ſhall you ſubtract the one totall from the other (I meane the leſſer from the greater) and the Remainer ſhall be your diuidend, ſo muſte you abate the leſſer error out of the greater, and the reſidue ſhal be the diuiſour. Now diuide the diuidend by that diuiſour, and the quotient will ſhew you the true number that you ſéeke for: But and if the errours be vnlike then muſt you adde both thoſe totalles (whych you noted) togy[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ther and take that whole number for the di[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]uidend, ſo ſhall you adde both the errours to[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]gither, and that whole number ſhall be the diuiſour, and the quotient of that Diuiſion ſhall giue you the true number that the que[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſtion ſéeketh for: and thys is the whole rule.

So were it. But this ſhall you marke,☜ Note: that of what nature ſo euer the two poſitions be, of the ſame nature is the quotient. There[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]fore when the poſitions in this queſtion are 12 and 16,The profe of this rule. which both being numbers of the playing dayes, the quotiente ſhall declare the true numbers of playing dayes, where as if the poſitions had bene 28 and 24, whyche are ſuppoſed to be the working dayes, then woulde the quotient declare the true number of the working dayes, & not of playing dayes as it will doe nowe. And therefore to con[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tinue the worke of this queſtion, and to find the true number of playing dayes, I muſte multiplie croſſe wayes the firſte poſition 12 by 55, that is the ſeconde erroure, and the totall will be 660, then I multiplie 275 by 16, and it yéeldeth 4400. Now bicauſe the er[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]rours are like, that is to ſaye, both too much, I muſte ſubtracte 660, out of 4400, and ſo remaineth 3740, whiche is the diuidend. A[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]gaine I muſt ſubtract the leſſer errour 55 out of 275 that is the greater errour, and there wil remaine 220, which ſhall be the diuiſor, then diuiding 3740 by 220, the quotient wil be 17. Wherefore I ſaye nowe conſtantlie, that 17 is the true number of dayes that the Maſon played: and then it followeth, that he wrought 23 dayes, and ſo is the queſtion an[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſwered.

Nowe for the order of triall of this worke there néedeth none other proofe but only thys, to worke with this number according to the queſtion, and if it agrée, then appeareth the number to be it that you would haue. As here nowe ſéeing he wrought 23 daies, and muſte haue for euerie day 25 pence, the whole ſum commeth to 575. Then again ſéeing he play[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ed 17 dayes, and muſte abate 30 pence for e[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ueriedaye, the whole ſumme of the abate[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ment will be 510: therefore I ſubtracte 510 out of 575, and there wil remaine 65, which maketh 5 ſ, 5 d. the cleare wages of the Maſon for his worke, according to the que[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſtion.

Nowe muſt I mul[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tiplie [GAP:math] in croſſe wayes 220, by 30, and it will be 66000. Then againe I multiplie 330 by 20, and it will be alſo 6600. Where[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]fore if I ſhall ſubtract the one out of ye other, there will remaine nothing to be the Diui[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]dend.

In this you forget your ſelfe again: for in as much as the ſignes in the errors be vn[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]like, therefore muſt you worke by Addition, adding togither thoſe two totals to make the diuidend, and alſo adding the two errours to make the diuiſor. You meane, that if the errours haue like ſignes, then muſte the diuidend and the diuiſor be made by Subtraction, as is taught before: And if thoſe ſignes be vnlike (as in this laſte example they be) then muſte I by Addition gather the Diuidend and the diui[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſor. Therefore firſt I imagine that he boughte 20 yeardes of Damaſke, for which he ſhould paye after the former price 240 ſhillings: then muſte he néedes haue of veluet other 20 yeardes (to make vp the 40 yeardes) and that woulde coſte 400 ſ. And be[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]cauſe the ſignes of the errors be like, I muſt worke by ſubtraction: therfore I ſubtract 240 out of [GAP:illegible]60 and there reſteth 120, whiche is the diuidend: then doe I ſubtract 10 out of 18 by the ſame reaſon, and ſo is the diuiſor 8, which is found 15 times in 120, therefore I ſay that the firſt man did owe 15 lb, and then the ſecond man muſte owe 32 lb, for thoſe 2 doe make 47 lb, and the third man his debt is 56 for ſo much remaineth if I bate 15 out of 71, or if I take 32 out of 88.

And multiplie in croſſe ways 1775-1750- 1775 by 24, whereof commeth 42600. Alſo I multiplie 1750 by 12, and there ariſeth 21000. And bicauſe the ſignes are like, I doe ſubtract the one from the other, and ſo remai[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]neth the diuidend, 21600: then do I ſubtracte 1750 out of 1775, and there reſteth 25: by whiche I diuide 21600, and the quotiente is 864, wherof the halfe is 432, and the thyrde part is 288, the quarter is 216, which [GAP:math] all being added togither, will make 1800. And if you adde thereto the tenth which was abated before, then wil the whole ſum be 2000. And nowe doeth there come a queſtion to my memorie which was demaunded of me, but I was not able to anſwere to it, and now me thinketh I could ſolue it

[GAP:math] Theſe both er[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]rours wyth their poſitions I ſette downe as you ſée, and multiplie in croſſe 6825 by 1000, & it maketh 6825000. Then I multiplie 6650 by 500, and it doeth amounte to 3325000, whiche ſumme I doe ſubtract out of the firſte and there remaineth 3500000 as the diuidende. Alſo I doe ſub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tracte the leſſer error out of the greater, and ſo remaineth 175, by which I diuide the ſaid diuidend, and the quotient wil be 20000, ſo that I ſée, that by this rate he yt hathe 7000 acres of grounde, may kéepe 20000 ſhéepe: and thereby I coniecture, that many menne may kéepe ſo many ſhéepe, for many men (as the common talke) haue ſo manye acres of ground.

If it be ſo, then am I out of my greateſt doubt Then I ioine that 90 (which I founde as the halfe of the latter partition) vnto 48, which is left with the one man, and ſo hath he 138, whiche (I may ſay) is 18 too ma[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ny for the leaſt ſhould be but 120: that error doe I note, and then make a newe poſition, ſuppoſing the one man to haue 204, and the other to haue 96, wherefore of the 204 there muſt be laide downe 153, and ſo remaineth with him 51. Alſo of the 96 there muſte bée laid downe ⅛, that is 32, and ſo reſteth with that man. 64. Nowe of the 153 and 32 I make one ſumme as 185, whiche I muſte diuide into 2 equall partes. and ſo eche man ſhall haue 92 ½, wherevnto if I adde their former portions reſerued, then the one ſhall haue 156 ½ and the other hath 145 ½. Wher[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]fore I take the leſſer ſumme nowe agayne, as I did before, that is 143 ½, and finde that he hath too many by 23 ½, for he ſhoulde haue but 120, ſo haue I for my two poſitions two errors, which I ſet down, [GAP:math] as here may be ſeene, eche errour vnder his poſition, and then by the rule I doe multiplye in croſſe wayes 108 by 23 ½ and there riſeth 2538 whiche I note then againe I multiplye 96 by 18, and thereof amounteth 1728. Now becauſe the ſignes are both like, that is bothe too ma[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ny, I muſt work be Subtraction, and ſo aba[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ting 1728 out of 2538, there wil reſte for the diuidend 810: then for the diuiſor I ſubtract 18 out of 23 ½ and there remaineth 5 ½, by whiche I diuide 810, and the quotient will be 147 [GAP:illegible]/33[GAP:illegible], which is the iuſt portion of him that had the leaſt ſumme. And if I doe ſub[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]tracte it out of 300 being the totall ſumme, then wil there remaine 152 9/1[GAP:illegible], as the portion that the other did get.

Again, I multiply 204 by 18, & it maketh 3672, whiche I doe ſubtracte out of 4512, becauſe the ſignes be like, & there reſteth 840 for the diuidend: then ſubtracting 18 out of 23 ½, there will remaine 5 ½, which I muſt take for the Diuiſor. And ſo diuiding 840 by 5 ½, the quotient wil be 152 8/11, whereby I haue found an agréeable ſumme to that whiche I found by the former poſitions, for hym that had moſte, whiche if I doe ſubtracte out of 300, that is the totall, there wil reſt 147 [GAP:illegible]/11, which was the portion of him that hadde the leaſt parte.

Anſwer[CHAR:char:punc] The readie money [GAP:math] is neuer multiplyed: then ¼ multiplyed by 2 monthes as you did before, maketh ½ then ½ by 4 produceth 2 monthes, as appeareth here in the mar[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]gent: But nowe for the reſt of the money you can not multi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]plye it vntill you haue ſought what proportion it beareth to 800 lb. Therefore you muſt ſubtract the rea[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]die money: the ¼ and the 1/[GAP:illegible] out of the princi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]pall: The reſt wil be 66 ⅔ lb: which you muſt looke what parte it beareth to the principal, which you ſhal finde to be 1/12: The ſame you muſt alſo multiply by his time 12 monthes. And it yéeldeth 1 month: So all make 3 ½ monthes as appeareth in the margent.

Aunſwer. You may ſaye if 3 ⅓ ſ giue 4 ſ what will 100 lb giue? But then when you haue ſound you muſt ſubtract the product out of 100 lb, the reſt is your neate gaine: Or elſe to produce the neate gaine in your worke at the firſte: Then ſubtract the iuſt price out of the ouer price, as I taught before in the firſte beginning of loſſe and gain: And your conclu[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſion ſhal be al one, multiply & diuide by whi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ch of the two wayes you thinke good, and you ſhal find that he gaineth 16 lb 13 ſ 4 d in the 100 pound.

Anſwer. For as muche as the Factor ta[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]keth ⅖ of the gaine, he taketh ⅔ of that which the Merchant taketh: for ⅖ are the ⅔ of ⅗. And therefore the Factors laying in, ought to bée 400 pounde, which is ⅔ of 600 pounde that the Merchant laid in: Then Subtract 250, whiche the Factour did laye in from 400 pounde whiche ſhoulde haue bene his whole ſtocke: And there remaineth 150 pound: For the eſtimation of his perſon.

Anſwer Item, for the working of thys queſtion and ſuche other the like, you muſte vnderſtande, if the partie ouerſelling his wares require to haue alſo ſome portion in readye money: as [GAP:math] &c. Then ſhall you rebate the ſame demaunded part whatſoeuer it be from the ouer price And alſo from the iuſte price. And thoſe two numbers that ſhal remaine after the ſubtraction is made, ſhall be the two firſt numbers in the Rule of thrée. And the iuſte price of the ſame merchandiſe ſhall be the thirde number, whiche by the operation of the Rule of thrée directe ſhall yeelde you a true ſolution: howe and at what price, you ſhal ouerſel that your merchandiſe to ſaue your ſelfe harmeleſſe, and make the barter equal.

Take the ⅓ (of eightéene) which is the ouerprice of his cloth: which ⅓ of eightéen: is ſixe, whiche as appeareth here in the margent you muſt ſubtract [GAP:math] from 18: there reſteth 12. And alſo abate it from 14 which is the iuſte price of the cloth: and there remai[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]neth 8: which 8 and 12, are the two firſte numbers in the Rule of thrée. Then take 8 groates or 2 [GAP:illegible]/1 ſhillings for the third nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke] [CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ber. Then ſay by the Rule of thrée directe: if 8 ſ giue 12 ſ what ſhall 2 ⅔ ſ giue? Multiply and diuide, and you ſhal finde 4 ſ: And for ſo much ſhal the ſecond Mercha[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]t ſel his Ginger, or his commoditie in bar[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ter, to ballaunce the ſame equal.

Anſwere. Say, if 100 giue 110, what ſhall 40 ſ giue, which is the iuſte price of the dozen of ſtockings? multiplie, and diuide, and you ſhall finde 44 ſ: Then take the ¼ of 30 ſ whiche is 7 ſ — 6 d: And ſubtracte it from 25 ſ, and alſo from 30 ſ: And there will remaine 17 ſ — 6— and 22 ſ — 6 d, for the two firſte numbers in the Rule of thrée: and 44 ſ which is the iuſt price (with his gaine in the dozen of ſtockings) for the thirde number: Then multiplie and diuide, and you ſhall finde 56 ſ — 6 6/7: and for ſo muche he is to ſell his dozen of ſtockings in barter.

Anſwer. You muſte firſte ſéeke what is loſt vpon ye 100 lb, which to do you may ſay if you pleaſe, if 100 lb looſe 10? what ſhal 6 ⅔ ſ looſe? worke and you ſhall finde ⅔ ſhillings (or eight pence) whiche muſte be rebated from 6 ſ 8 d: So reſteth 6 ſhillings ſtill: or you may ſay if 100 lb giue me but 90 lb what ſhal 6 ſ 8 d giue? Worke this waye either and you ſhall finde alſo as before, directly in your quotient 6 ſ: your deſire. Then are you next to caſt vp what the 720 elles of Ca[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]brick commeth to at 6 ſ 8 d the ell and you ſhall finde 240 pounde: the ½ whereof the Cam[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]bricke Merchaunt wil haue in readie money (which is 120 pound) nextly you muſte caſte what the Cambrick co[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]meth to after his loſſe in the 100 lb whiche as you founde is but 6 ſ an ell: and you ſhal find 216 lb: now muſt you ſubtract (his readie money which is 120 lb) out of 240 lb: & alſo of 216 lb. And there wil remaine 120 lb & 96 lb for your two firſt numbers in the Rule of thrée, and 30 ſ the o[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]uerprice of your Saffron for the third nu[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]ber. Then multiply and diuide, and you ſhal find 24 ſ: and ſo muche didde hys Saffron coſte in readie money.

IT is to be noted, that 7 pound Flemiſh maketh but 6 lb. ſterling, 7 ſ Flemiſhe, maketh 6 ſ ſterl. and 7 d flem. 6 d ſterl. So that 7 yéeldeth but 6. Wherin is euide[CHAR:char:cmbAbbrStroke]t, that there is loſt 1/7, (if it may be ſo called) when it is reduced into Engliſh money. Wherefore to know how much 233 lb. 13 ſ, 4 d, flemiſh maketh Engliſh, you muſt ſubtract from it 1/7, beginning with the pounds, &c. and that whi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]che reſteth after this ſubtraction is the ſum required: ſo that 233 lb, 13 ſ, 3 d flem. ma[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]keth 200 lb, 5 ſ, 8 4/7 d. ſterling.

Note that a lb ſterling, maketh 1 lb, 3 ſ, 4 d flem. that is 1 lb ⅙: 1 ſ ſter. maketh 1 ſ ⅙ flem. and 1 ſter. maketh 1 ⅙ Flem. So that there is gained (if it may ſo be called) ⅙ of the ſumme being thus reduced to Flem. For of 6/6 is made 7/6[CHAR:char:punc] which is 1 whole, and ⅙. Then to knowe how much 237 lb 7 ſ 6 d ſter. ma[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]keth Flem. ſubtract from your ſter. the ⅙ of the whole ſumme. and adde it to the ſame ſumme, and it maketh 276 lb 18 ſ 9 d, whi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]che is the ſumme required.

Nowe after he hath doubled his number, bid him adde therevnto 5 more, which done, bidde him multiply that his number by 5 al[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſo, whiche done, bidde him tell you the iuſte ſumme of his laſte Multiplication, whiche ſumme the giuer thinking it nothing auaile[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]able, becauſe it is ſo greate aboue his preten[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ded imagination: yet thereby ſhal you pre[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]ſently wyth the helpe of Subtraction tell his propoſed number.

But note, that when you haue made your ſubtraction, if there doe remaine a 0: in the place of tens, that is to ſay, in the ſeconde place, you muſt then abate 1, from that fi[CHAR:char:EOLhyphen]gure which is in the place of Hundreds, that is to wit from the figure which is next your left hand, and that ſhall be worth 10 tenths, ſignifying the tenth finger: as if there ſhould remaine 803, you muſt ſay, that the ſeuenth perſon vppon his tenth finger, and vppon his third ioint, hath the Ring.
